The checker refuses such a size outside its kind: 0 to 4294967295 for `nat`, and `ZZ32`'s range for `int`. Walk refuses it at run time, where it binds the size to a static parameter. Walk reads and computes a size exactly, with no wrap: it reads a size used as a value as a `ZZ32` up to 2^31-1 and as a `ZZ64` above. The checker types such a value `IntLiteral`. The compiled class loader checks no size that it computes at instantiation: `next[\nat k\]()`, which builds a `Box[\k + 1\]`, answers 4294967296 at `k = 4294967295` (gap-ledger row 675; F-222). Gated by `tests/NatBigSizeWalk` for walk's reading. The refusals are gated by `compiler_tests/XXXNatRangeChecker`, `XXXNatArithRangeChecker` and `NatRtBigSize`, and by `tests/XXXNatBeyondNN32Walk`, `XXXIntBeyondZZ32Walk`, `XXXIntBelowZZ32Walk`, `XXXNatArithProductWalk` and `XXXNatArithSumWalk`; each `XXX` test passes because its program is refused. Open under walk: an array of a static size from 2^31 to 2^32-1 stops at its store's factory, 'Closure/Constructor for makeJavaArrayStore parameter 1 (n:ZZ32) got type Long', where no catch sees it (row 527). Also open, as notes on row 325 (a numeral outside a bounded integer type): on the compiled path a `nat` size above `ZZ32`'s range, used where a `ZZ32` is needed, as in a range, fails at run time, as a numeral beyond `ZZ32` does, and neither P-40 nor the specification says where such a size is refused; and under walk a `ZZ32`-declared return passes such a size on as a `ZZ64`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-size-range/REPORT.md` sections 6 and 12.

- F-151 **In the interpreter's library, `Vector`, `Matrix` and their factories and operators bound their element type by `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`.** `Number` declares no arithmetic, so the compiled checker accepts the bodies' arithmetic only through `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`. `Number` stays in the bound, though it has no `comprises` clause now (F-324). The four juxtapositions of a vector or a matrix with a scalar `T`, in either order, stand beside the library's juxtapositions with a `String`, and the checker finds no error in them (F-53); no run measures what now keeps a scalar `T` apart from `String`. The vector norm is declared at each of the eight number types, by its own `asFloat` (F-324). The eight number types meet the bound. `Number` itself and the numeral type `IntLiteral` do not, since neither is a ring at its own type. So `Vector[\Number,n\]` is not a well-formed type, and `array1` and `array2` have no branch for `Number`: called at `Number`, they give a plain array at run time, not a vector or a matrix (F-229). The checker accepts a call whose argument's type is built from the caller's own type parameter under the same bound, such as the norm's `squaredNorm(me)` (F-227). The scalar extension, the eight operators between an array and a scalar, has bounds of its own, also with `Number` (F-119). Gated under walk by `tests/ArrayElementAlgebra.fss`. The bound is the default that `reviews/array-fork2-judgement.md` recommended. It landed when the curator said to land it. Detail: that judgement, sections 2.5 (what `Number`'s `comprises` clause gives), 2.9, way 3 (the ring alone, measured) and 4 (the bound and its cost).

- F-278 **The library's subscripts over a generic index type are a valid overloading at every instance: the index parameter is bounded by `Index`, which `ZZ32` extends and the ranges exclude, and a tuple type whose element types are all `Index` types is an `Index`, outside `Object`, on both paths.** Under the full check of symbolic operators the 124 subscript errors of F-245 are gone and none comes (191 to 67 with this change alone, on climb batch 21's base, F-245); the stock count (3) and distance (5) do not move. Gated by `tests/TupleIndexBoundWalk.fss` and, for walk's exclusion, `tests/TupleIndexExclusionWalk.fss` with its `.test`; the checker's half by the distance stage, which checks every operator (F-281). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-index-bound/REPORT.md` sections 1, 5 and 6.

(* Under walk, a generic built from a number or string value is built at the value's trait, ZZ32, RR64 or String, also inside a tuple, and walk's type text names the trait. *)
component LanguageTypeInstancesWalk
import List.{...}
import Reflect.{...}
export Executable

object Cell[\T extends Any\](v: T) end

kind(c: Cell[\ZZ32\]): String = "ZZ32"
kind(c: Cell[\RR64\]): String = "RR64"
kind(c: Cell[\String\]): String = "String"
kind(c: Any): String = "Any"

filled[\T\](x: T): Array[\T,ZZ32\] = array[\T\](3).fill(x)

openAt[\I\](x: I): OpenRange[\I\] = openRange[\I\]()

run(): () = do
    z: ZZ32 = 3
    r: RR64 = asFloat(z)
    assert(kind(Cell(z)), "ZZ32", "Cell(z) for z: ZZ32 is a Cell[\\ZZ32\\] and runs the declaration over Cell[\\ZZ32\\] (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert(kind(Cell(3)), "ZZ32", "Cell(3) is a Cell[\\ZZ32\\] and runs the declaration over Cell[\\ZZ32\\] (literals.tex, section \"Literals\"; inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert(kind(Cell(r)), "RR64", "Cell(r) for a computed r: RR64 is a Cell[\\RR64\\] and runs the declaration over Cell[\\RR64\\] (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert(kind(Cell("s")), "String", "Cell(\"s\") is a Cell[\\String\\] and runs the declaration over Cell[\\String\\] (literals.tex, section \"Literals\")")
    assert(instanceOf[\Cell[\ZZ32\]\](Cell(3)), true, "Cell(3) is an instance of Cell[\\ZZ32\\] (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert(instanceOf[\Cell[\(ZZ32, String)\]\](Cell((z, "s"))), true, "Cell((z, \"s\")) is an instance of Cell[\\(ZZ32, String)\\] (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert(Just(3) = Just[\ZZ32\](3), true, "Just(3) is the Just[\\ZZ32\\] of 3 (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert(Just(z) = Just[\ZZ32\](z), true, "Just(z) for z: ZZ32 is the Just[\\ZZ32\\] of z (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert(SUM <|1, 2, 3|>, 6, "SUM of the list display <|1, 2, 3|> is 6 (aggregate.tex, section \"List Expressions\"; reductions.tex, section \"Summations and Other Reduction Expressions\")")
    assert(SUM <|z, z|>, 6, "SUM of the list display <|z, z|> for z: ZZ32 is 6 (reductions.tex, section \"Summations and Other Reduction Expressions\")")
    zs: List[\ZZ32\] = <|z, z|>
    assert(|zs|, 2, "the list display <|z, z|> for z: ZZ32 is a List[\\ZZ32\\] (aggregate.tex, section \"List Expressions\")")
    ss: List[\String\] = <|"a", "b"|>
    assert(|ss|, 2, "the list display <|\"a\", \"b\"|> is a List[\\String\\] (aggregate.tex, section \"List Expressions\"; literals.tex, section \"Literals\")")
    assert(instanceOf[\AnyVector\](filled(z)), true, "an array of three at a T inferred from a ZZ32 argument is a vector (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert(instanceOf[\OpenRange[\ZZ32\]\](openAt(z)), true, "the open range at an index type inferred from a ZZ32 argument is a ZZ32 open range (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert(typeOf(3).toString, "ZZ32", "the type of 3 prints as ZZ32")
    assert(typeOf(z).toString, "ZZ32", "the type of z: ZZ32 prints as ZZ32")
    assert(typeOf("s").toString, "String", "the type of \"s\" prints as String")
    assert(typeOf((z, "s")).toString, "(ZZ32,String)", "the type of the pair (z, \"s\") prints as (ZZ32,String)")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

\Library\ declare none of the constant traits.
An expression composed only of numerals and operators is folded, before the
static check and on both implementations, into a \emph{signed constant}, which
holds its value exactly and whose kind its operands give: computed from
numerals without a radix point and without a quotient, it is an integer,
written as an integer numeral or a negated one; computed from numerals without
a radix point with a quotient among its operations, it is a quotient, written as
the reduced quotient of two integer numerals; and computed from a numeral with a
radix point, it is written as a numeral with a radix point, or a negated one,
where its denominator divides a power of ten, and otherwise as the reduced
quotient of two numerals whose numerator has a radix point.
Where nothing fixes the type of a signed constant (\secref{literals}), an
integer takes the default of an integer numeral, a quotient the type
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, and a constant computed from a numeral with a radix point the
type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, whatever its value, so that \EXP{6/3} is a
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{0.5 + 0.5} an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}; where a place fixes
a type, the constant is converted into it as a numeral is, with at most one
rounding.

A numeral is converted where it stands, into the type that its place fixes,
and not before, because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect numerals to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it to a floating-point number before its place is known
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used where a floating-point interval is expected,
it is better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
----
\EXP{\VAR{op}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Number}\rrbracket(a\COLON{}T, b\COLON{}T)}
and \EXP{\VAR{op}(a\COLON\TYP{Any}, b\COLON\TYP{Any})}, the call
\EXP{\VAR{op}(z, w)}, where \VAR{z} has type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \VAR{w} has

coercion, since its instance at \TYP{Number} is, and is more specific than the
second; the first is instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \VAR{z} is coerced,
and the converted call runs that instance.

literal evaluated twice, and two literals of one text, are strictly equivalent;
a string that a program builds as it runs is another object than a literal of

(\secref{literals}).
\revision{revival-string-literals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 did not
say whether a string literal denotes one object.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that two string literals of one text are
one object, on both implementations; strings remain reference objects.}

== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

## 3. The forks, with their defaults

**Consequential** means what the `coordinator` skill's `SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions", gives: it reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of his; it touches microGPT's lines, speed or readability; it chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent; or it cannot be undone.

### The consequential forks

N1 (the numeral types as value objects with fields), N4 (point 3, `RadixPointNumeral`'s `asFloat`), and F5 to F7 taken together are in section 2. Each is below with its rung, at its default.

### Forks the batch takes

Each default can be undone and none reverses a decision of his; none touches a model line. Where the record leaves a choice open, the default follows the team's source or the library's way, which the fork names. Those marked **(consequential)** are the three of section 2.
15. **N7. Where walk converts, and how.** At a chosen declaration's parameter, a typed binding, a field and a declared return type, the checker's places, a numeral converts from its exact value: into the eight number types in walk's Java, by the same conversion as the library's coercion, a numeral out of the type's range refused at the place when it runs, as walk refuses one at a binding today (row 325's walk half); into a numeral type as the numeral object; into a program's type through its coercion from the numeral type, called with the numeral object, its result kept for the site so that a site gives one object (review-queue item 440's default); else refused. Default: so. The ways not taken: a numeral object at every evaluation, which every `i + 1` would pay; conversion at bindings and fields only, as P-172's text names, which would leave a return of `QQ`, `RR32`, `NN32` or `NN64` unconverted.

content.content:
\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
Or is that just part of lexical structure?
(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}

The radix of a numeral is ten, unless its digits are followed by an underscore
and a radix indicator (\secref{numerals}), which give its radix $r$; such a
numeral has the same type as one without an indicator.
So \EXP{\mathtt{deadc}_{16}} is a \TYP{NaturalNumeral} whose four numbers are
$5$, $0$, $16$ and $912092$.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 gave a numeral
the types \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket},
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket},
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket},
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket},
\EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket} for a numeral without leading zeros,
and \EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}, whose static arguments are
the four numbers.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that the four numbers are fields of the
numeral's value: the two types with an explicit radix fold into the radix, and
\TYP{Literal} into the digit count, which tells whether a numeral has leading
zeros.
So the team's draft notes above are answered: two numerals of one kind have one
type, which holds every such numeral, and \TYP{Numeral} comprises the two
numeral types.}
(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of
digits) then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$ be the
radix) has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}
where $v$ is
the value of the $n$-digit numeral interpreted in radix $r$.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point) has type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is
the value of the numeral, with the radix point deleted,
interpreted in radix ten.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point), then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$
be the radix) has the following type:
\begin{Fortress}
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
\end{Fortress}
where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.

Every numeral also has type
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}.

content.content:
+- F-342 **The compiled checker converts a numeral where nothing fixes a type into its default, refuses one out of range, and refuses a numeral type written other than as a parameter's type.** Where no place's type has a coercion from the numeral's type or is a numeral type (an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter, a receiver, a join, a result with no declared return type), a numeral becomes a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its value, or an `RR64` with a radix point; a type parameter that numerals alone fix takes the narrowest default holding them all; the conversion into the default ranks as no coercion; a numeral outside a bounded number type's range, or rounding to an infinity, is a static error, also as a tuple's element at a tuple type; a program's type with no coercion from the numeral's type refuses a numeral; `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` are written in a program only as a parameter's type; a `nat` or `int` parameter read as a value is a `ZZ32`. It builds P-173's checker, P-174's written-only rule and P-40's size value; a `typecase`'s selector keeps the numeral's type (row 963). Tests: `compiler_tests/LiteralDefaultCompiled`, `LiteralDefaultResultCompiled`, `XXXLiteralTypeUnwritable.test`, `XXXNumeralBeyondZZ32Range.test`, `XXXNumeralBeyondRangeInTuple.test`, `NatValueZZ32Compiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-checker/REPORT.md`, "1. What changed and why".
+- F-340 **On the compiled path a numeral at a typed place of `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `RR64` or `RR32` is that type's constant, a float rounded once, and a program's coercion from a numeral runs once per site, in the component class's static initializer.** The coercion desugarer types the numeral at the place's type (`compiler/desugarer/CoercionDesugarer.scala`), and the code generator emits the type's `make` with a float from `roundToDouble` or `roundToFloat` (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java`), so `x: RR64 = 0.9999999999999999` is below 1.0; each site's coercion result is a static field `numeral$coercion$N` of the component's class, and a coercion that raises stops the program before `run()`. A program's generic type is not hoisted (row 957). Tests: `compiler_tests/FloatNumeralOneRounding.test`, `NumeralCoercionOnceCompiled.test`, `NumeralCoercionRaisesCompiled.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-literal-fold/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".
+- F-343 **Two string literals of one text are one object on both paths, and a concatenation by `||` of string and character literals is one string literal before the checker.** Walk interns a literal's text and compares two flat strings by the Java strings they carry (`interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java`, `forStringLiteralExpr`; `values/FString.java`, `seqv`); the compiled path loads a literal with `ldc` and `equality.sEquiv` compares two `FJavaString`s' carried strings by `==` (`nativeHelpers/equalityRule.java`); the pre-typecheck desugaring that both paths run folds infix `||` of string literals, or of string and character literals with a string among the first two (`compiler/desugarer/PreTypeCheckDesugaringVisitor.java`). So `"ab" SEQV "ab"`, `f() SEQV f()` for `f(): String = "ab"` and `("foo" || "bar") SEQV "foobar"` are `true`, and a string built at run time is a new object, except where Java answers the same string, as a whole slice does. A concatenation of literals is a flat literal, not a rope, so a test that needs a rope or a string built apart joins a literal with a variable. Tests: `tests/StringLiteralIdentityWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/StringLiteralIdentityCompiled.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-string-literals/REPORT.md`, sections 1, 4 and 8.

Open on the compiled path: through the prelude's `Object`, an object that declares or inherits a zero-argument Fortress member named `toString` overflows the stack when it is printed (row 321), though not through the one library's `Object`, whose `asString` is `self.ilkName`; and `asDebugString` and `asExprString` print differently from walk's, where the specification is silent (row 363). For a string static argument both paths give `Cell[\String\]`, the specification's answer, walk reading a string object at `String` (F-344). For a numeral argument neither path gives the specification's type. Gated by `compiler_tests/DefaultRenderRungS`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-default-rendering/REPORT.md`, "Defects and their homes".
+- F-228 **Under walk, a reduction or a comprehension that writes no static argument instantiates its big operator by a declared type, else by the join of its elements' run-time types, else at its bound, where an F-bounded parameter stays open.** It builds P-48. The declared type is a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's declared return type, for either also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a top-level variable, a field, an assignment, a function expression, a branch, a call's argument and another clause form's body do not direct it. Otherwise the clauses run once into the library's collector, `__elemsOf`, which keeps the elements in order, typed at the join of their run-time types, and the operator is instantiated at that join; the reduction then runs over the collected elements, so each body runs once. A declared type or a join that does not fit falls back to the instance that no hint gives: a plain-bounded parameter takes its bound, and an F-bounded one stays open (F-143). So a `SUM` of `ZZ32` and `RR64` values, whose join `Number` is outside the bound, runs with each `+` at its operands' types. The same holds with no element and no declared type. With the big operator so instantiated, the library types `__bigOperator`'s local function `body(i: I)` at the element type `I`. A big operator whose declared result is a trait of its own is read through the `BigReduction`, `Comprehension` or `BigOperator` that the trait extends (row 718, fixed). Still wrong, each a ledger row: an empty clause form that no declared type directs takes it
+- F-249 **Under walk, a program that imports only the prelude reaches the string objects' own `||` through the top-level `opr ||(a:String, b:String)`, whose `typecase` calls them.** The string objects' own `||` are those that the objects `FlatString` and `EmptyString` declare, and that the trait `Concatenable` declares for the objects `CatString` and `SubString`. `FortressLibrary`, where the top-level `||` is declared, sees them only where an api that it imports states them: `FlatString`'s api does, and String's api states `Concatenable`'s and `EmptyString`'s three each (`Library/String.fsi:17-19`, `:29-31`). +- F-253 **Under walk, a call of a generic method that writes no static argument infers the method's own static arguments from the arguments' run-time types.** This holds for a dotted call, as for a call of a generic function, whether the method is alone under its name or among its receiver's overloads. Among the receiver's overloads, where one of two is a generic dotted method and exactly one of their declared domains lies inside the other, walk chooses the inner one; otherwise it compares them on the instance that the call makes (F-252). A generic method that a trait declares reads its bounds, and the types to which its arguments convert, in the trait's method environment, where its instances bind and evaluate their types, as a method that an object declares does. So it takes the instance that the same method declared in an object takes: a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` give `Box[\ZZ64\]` with the `ZZ32` converted, and a bounded type parameter that nothing fixes takes its bound. A generic functional method that an object inherits from a trait is chosen beside the object's plain one where only it applies. This inference lets the team's generic 
+- F-229 **`array1` and `array2` give a vector and a matrix only at the eight number types, chosen by a `typecase` over a witness of their result type; at any other element type they give a plain array.** The branches are `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64`; each builds the array at that type and returns it through `cast`, in `additiveIdentity`'s shape. `Array1` and `Array2` are invariant, so a branch matches only its own number type exactly. `Number` and `AnyIntegral` get a plain array, since `Vector[\Number,n\]` is not well-formed under the element bound `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }` of `Vector` and `Matrix` (F-151).
